items.title: Why AI systems are most useful as designers of new scientific tools
items.author: James Evans
items.blurb: Reviewing Alexander Krauss's The Engine of Scientific Discovery, Evans argues that because breakthroughs historically follow new instruments, AI's largest contribution to science may be designing the next generation of them rather than producing findings itself.

items.title: How New Zealand’s biggest city solved its housing crisis
items.blurb: Rezoning reshaped New Zealand's largest city — the clearest test yet of whether upzoning fixes housing, though the FT notes critics doubt the lesson transfers.

items.title: Economists should be worried about birth rates
items.author: Noah Smith
items.blurb: Smith pushes back on economists who wave away falling fertility, arguing that an aging and shrinking population is a threat worth taking seriously.

items.title: AI tool lets researchers 'vibe code' in the quantum realm
items.author: Davide Castelvecchi
items.blurb: An autonomous agent now writes and executes quantum-computing code on its own, though Castelvecchi reports it still needs a human hand at points.

items.title: Some fertility and AI forecasts
items.author: Tyler Cowen
items.blurb: Cowen flags a new fertility projection on which global GDP in 2100 is 10 percent lower, payroll taxes to fund old-age benefits are far higher, and China's share of world output falls from 25.6 to 14.9 percent while America's rises from 11.2 to 14.4 percent.

items.title: Africa Can't Afford to Squander Its Demographic Opportunity
items.author: Jakkie Cilliers
items.blurb: Cilliers argues that the age structure of a population, more than corruption or weak institutions, is the strongest single predictor of growth, stability, and democratic consolidation across African countries.

items.title: Exclusive: NSF set to issue lowest number of new grants in four decades
items.author: Dan Garisto
items.blurb: The US science-funding agency is withholding $1 billion of its budget so the money can go to a special White House project, leaving it on track for its fewest new grants in four decades.

items.title: A China Strategy That Lasts
items.author: Bill Cassidy
items.blurb: Cassidy argues that a China policy durable enough to outlast a single administration has to be written by Congress rather than improvised by the executive.

items.title: Staggering 90% of biomedical papers now show signs of AI help
items.author: Kaia Glickman
items.blurb: Papers published in December and archived in PubMed show signs of large-language-model help at a rate far above previous estimates.

items.title: South Africa's scientists must register with official body or risk prison, according to draft law
items.author: Sarah Wild
items.blurb: A draft South African law would require researchers to register with a regulatory body on pain of prison, and Wild finds many of the scientists it covers have not heard of it.

items.title: NIH proposes major revamp of how it scores research grant proposals
items.author: Max Kozlov
items.blurb: For five decades the NIH reported the exact numerical peer-review score of each proposal; the new plan reports only a top, middle or bottom tier, which proponents call an honest admission that three reviewers cannot support that precision and critics call cover for political interference.

items.title: Democracies Need Creative Destruction
items.author: Jennifer Pahlka & Andrew Greenway
items.blurb: Argues that dissatisfaction with democracy is partly a delivery problem: governments accumulate procedures they never retire, as when US pandemic surveillance spending failed to detect COVID for a month because labs could not get permission to test swabs.

items.title: How China Found Its Most Potent Weapon
items.author: Gloria Xiong & Jessica Chen Weiss
items.blurb: Deng Xiaoping's 1992 line that China has rare earths as the Middle East has oil is now read in Washington as a decades-old coercive plan; the authors reconstruct how the dominance was actually built.

items.title: Indian cities should embrace skyscrapers
items.blurb: Local rules keep Indian cities low-rise; Hyderabad is the counterexample the Economist uses to argue the restrictions are self-defeating.

items.title: China will struggle to make money from humanoid robots
items.blurb: China is ahead of its rivals on humanoid robots and is training thousands of them, but the Economist finds profits are still a long way off.

items.title: Another Big Difference Between Liberals and Conservatives
items.author: Olga Khazan
items.blurb: People on the right tend to have more children than people on the left; Khazan asks what explains the gap.

items.title: The Case for Chilling Out About Birth Rates
items.author: Idrees Kahloon
items.blurb: Kahloon grants that the fertility decline is real and probably persistent, then argues its consequences fall well short of the catastrophe the pronatalist case assumes.

items.title: How to Lose a Trade War
items.author: David Frum
items.blurb: David Frum reads the collapse of the US–Canada talks as evidence that coercion is a poor instrument of trade policy.

items.title: Are we watching the U.S. go bankrupt?
items.author: Noah Smith
items.blurb: Noah Smith answers no, then sets out which fiscal pressures actually warrant concern.

items.title: Two toots for England’s planning overhaul
items.blurb: The Economist calls Labour's planning overhaul a genuinely bold supply-side reform, though it withholds the third cheer.

items.title: Chinese firms are wrapping their supply chains around the globe
items.blurb: An interactive account of Chinese manufacturers relocating production abroad, rewiring global supply chains rather than retreating from them.

items.title: What Really Happens If China Wins the AI Race?
items.author: Matteo Wong
items.blurb: The tech industry has portrayed Chinese AI development as an existential threat for years; Wong argues what would actually follow from Chinese models leading is less straightforward than that framing implies.

items.title: Has the European turnaround finally arrived?
items.author: Tyler Cowen
items.blurb: Earnings per share at Stoxx Europe 600 firms rose 18% year-on-year in the second quarter after two flat years; Cowen asks whether that marks a turn.

items.title: China’s Alibaba plans $10.2bn share placement in AI push
items.blurb: Alibaba is raising $10.2bn for its AI push after a strong reception for its Qwen 3.8-Max model.
